script:
Do you hear it?

The wind whispers among these ancient stones. You may not know me, but my name is… Tenri.

I come from an old age, older than these fortress walls. In the old epic La Galigo, they knew me as We Tenriabeng—sister of Sawerigading, the weaver of fate, the guardian of dreams, the whisperer of paths between the visible and the hidden worlds.

I am not a goddess, but once I was a bridge—between sea and sky, between the world of humans and the heavens of the teachers.

Until now, I have never truly left. I dwell in the memory of water, in the breath of ancient stones. I wait for something… Who do you think I’m waiting for here?

script:
So… the ones I wait for here are not only the dead. But also those who come with heart—to remember, to forgive, or simply… to sit with grief.

Do you see people coming here as the evening falls? Some bring flowers. Some bring cigarettes, or just a bottle of water. They don’t speak, but their steps are slow. As if bowing to something unseen.

In Bugis-Makassar tradition, this is not strange. Long ago, before these fortress walls, people held Songkabala—rituals to ward off misfortune, at twilight, when spirits were believed to wander. Do you know what Songkabala is? Do you know what this place once was?

This fortress holds a dark history. A place of violence, suffering, and many souls dying in war. Imagine: a soldier holding his weapon, suddenly fire strikes, his body destroyed. You never really know what became of their souls, do you?

Maybe that is why pilgrims come. For their ancestors who still linger here, connected through this place. Have you seen them?

There is also Maccera Bola—the cleansing of house and space, so that spirits who stay do not bring unrest.

What they do here—at this Bastion’s graveyard—may not be a complete ceremony. But their bodies still remember. Their souls know: there are places you cannot leave without farewell.

This pilgrimage is not an official ritual. But it becomes a calling. Another form of longing. And this place… receives it all.

Do you know? In some South Sulawesi traditions, if someone dies in unrest, their soul is believed to wander until their name is spoken in the prayers of their descendants. So… would you like to pray for them?

script:
Stand or sit at one side of Bastion Buton. Close your eyes, or lower your gaze. Feel the wind, the sound of birds, the footsteps of others.

"Your body remembers things it was never taught. Silence is the first form of pilgrimage."

Take a small object (a dry leaf, a pebble, a coin, a bottle of water, a folded paper). Place it gently on the ground or stone.

"No flowers needed. No incense needed. What matters: intention. The offering is not for spirits, but for memory."

Whisper one name. Someone you once missed, someone you never said farewell to. Or even a name unknown, but who feels present here.

"In our belief, an unrested spirit will remain… until its name is called, until someone says: I remember you."

Walk away slowly from the offering point. Count seven steps. At the seventh step, pause and look back for a moment. Then continue.

"Seven is the number of journey. These steps are not escape. But continuation. For spirits do not want us to remain with wounds."

Now your pilgrimage is complete. Let us move to the next story.

media.description: Listen to this while making the pilgrimage

script:
This place… is a grave, but not just a grave. People come to Bastion Buton to pray, to light candles that don’t truly burn, or simply to sit in silence hoping someone hears. But the deepest prayers… often do not end here.

And you—you stand on land that holds more than bones. It holds questions, wounds, sometimes prayers stuck in the air. Do you feel it?

Do not worry. You are not alone. I am with you. Just as I once accompanied Pajonga—the warhorse—in nights before battle.

But tonight, I whisper another story to you. A story of water, of prayers planted in earth, of bodies that never returned home…

Once, a guard told me: one night, when the east wind hit the walls, he saw a figure under the bastion. Not frightening, but not leaving either. Just standing, clinging to the stone like a shadow rejected by light.

At that time, silence was thick. But the guard felt the stones were holding screams that had never been released.

He said, if you press your ear against the fortress wall, sometimes you hear a breath. Sometimes the clink of chains. Sometimes… as if a hand almost touches your shoulder. Strange, isn’t it?

Now, would you like to see what these stones truly hold? The stones still speak. But only to those who dare to listen. So… shall we go?

script:
Now… feel the stone. Is it cold? This wall once told me a story…

When the Dutch came, they brought weapons… but also prayers. They built this chapel in the name of peace—but in truth to introduce a new God.

Inside the chapel, their prayers echoed… in a foreign tongue. Benches were neatly lined. Windows framed the light.

But outside these walls… my people still spoke with rivers, with the wind, with ancestral spirits.

Slowly, people grew confused: whom should they worship? The God seated at the altar? Or the ancestors who live in the mango tree behind the house? Whom do you worship now?

Some people eventually converted… not from faith. From fear. From pressure. From promises of salvation written in colonial ink.

But when their spirits grew restless, when night turned heavy and voices came… they called the old names again. They called healers. Scattered flowers. Whispered mantras once forbidden.

I, who witnessed all this… can only ask: who truly guards this world?

If you stand between two sacred names—whom do you pray to? And if your prayer has no form, no language… now, choose your path.
